name: Erythropoietin
lead: Erythropoietin (EPO) is a glycoprotein hormone made mainly by the kidneys in response to low oxygen; it stimulates red blood cell production in the bone marrow. Its gene is switched on by hypoxia-inducible factors, and it signals through the EPO receptor and JAK2 [1][2][4][11].

Recombinant human EPO (epoetin alfa, first approved by the US FDA in 1989 according to Grokipedia) is used to treat anaemia of chronic kidney disease and chemotherapy-related anaemia [11]. In sport and fitness communities it is known as an endurance-boosting performance drug because raising red cell mass increases oxygen-carrying capacity. Its connection to appearance runs via the muscle and body-composition culture in which it is sometimes mentioned.

Beyond erythropoiesis, laboratory research has examined EPO as a neuroprotective agent, reporting that it crosses the blood-brain barrier in animals and reduces ischaemic brain injury [3][7][8]. Grokipedia notes that medical use has raised safety concerns, including increased mortality and serious cardiovascular events in some patient groups [11].

paras: EPO binds its receptor on erythroid progenitor cells, which lack their own kinase domain; binding triggers phosphorylation and activation of JAK2, driving survival, proliferation and maturation [4][11]. Production is regulated by oxygen: under hypoxia the transcription factor HIF-1 binds an enhancer of the EPO gene, and HIF-1 was found to be a general mediator of hypoxic transcription in many cell types [1][2][5]. HIF-2 alpha is described as the dominant isoform in kidney EPO production [11].

Animal studies reported that systemically given recombinant EPO reduced focal ischaemic brain injury and that EPO receptors are present at brain capillaries [3][8]. Other work reported anti-apoptotic signalling involving Jak2 and NF-kappaB [10][7]. A 2002 paper reported that EPO therapy for acute stroke was safe and beneficial [9].

Registered clinical trials of EPO products are largely in anaemia. They include phase 3 comparisons of biosimilar epoetin alfa with the reference product in chronic kidney disease and dialysis patients [12][15][16], long-term safety studies of a further epoetin [14][18], and trials of epoetin in leukemia and chemotherapy-related anaemia [17][19][20]. A phase 2 study begun in 1993 examined the time course of EPO activity in renal failure [21]. These registrations concern patients with disease; none in the sources reviewed tests EPO for appearance or looksmaxxing goals in healthy people.

Grokipedia reports that medical use of recombinant EPO has been associated with increased mortality, serious cardiovascular events such as heart attack and stroke, and other risks in some patient populations [11]. The source reviewed gives limited detail, and readers should consult drug labels for authoritative safety information.
EPO is a prescription drug and its use for performance enhancement is prohibited in competitive sport. The sources reviewed contain no documented looksmaxxing-forum discussion of EPO.

timeline.event: Epoetin alfa approved by the US FDA [11].
JAK2 shown to be activated by EPO receptor stimulation [4].
Systemic EPO reported to cross the blood-brain barrier and protect against experimental brain injury in animals [3].

card.summary: A kidney hormone and anaemia drug used for endurance doping; indirect link to appearance, with serious cardiovascular warnings.
card.note: Prescription drug banned in sport; linked to cardiovascular events in some patient groups.

quick.overview:
Erythropoietin is the hormone that tells bone marrow to make red blood cells. Injectable versions treat anaemia in kidney disease and chemotherapy patients.

It is known mostly as an endurance-sport doping agent. The sources reviewed describe clinical trials in anaemic patients and none aimed at appearance.
quick.mechanism: It binds the EPO receptor on red-cell precursors, activating JAK2 signalling to increase red blood cell production. The body releases it more when oxygen is low.
quick.risks: It is an Rx-only drug. Reported risks in patients include cardiovascular events and increased mortality in some groups; it is banned in competitive sport.
